questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Curvature of a Curve at a Point
questions.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=⟨{e}^{t},\,{t}^{3},\,2t⟩$ for $t\ge 0$, use the cross product curvature formula to compute the curvature at the point $P(1,0,0).$
questions.worked_solution:
The curvature $κ(t)$ is given by

$$
κ(t)=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}.
$$

First, we find the value of $t$ that corresponds to the point $P(1,0,0)$ on the given curve. We know that

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨1,0,0⟩ \\ ⟨{e}^{t},\,{t}^{3},\,2t⟩ & =⟨1,0,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the respective components gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}{e}^{t}=1 \\ {t}^{3}=0 \\ 2t=0.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equality, $t=0.$ This value also satisfies the other two equations. Therefore, $P(1,0,0)$ is at the tip of $r(0).$ 

Now, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$, ${r}^{′}(0),$  and $‖{r}^{′}(0)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t)⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{t},\,3{t}^{2},\,2⟩ \\ {r}^{′}(0) & =⟨1,0,2⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(0)‖ & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{2}^{2}}=\sqrt{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find ${r}^{″}(t)$ and ${r}^{″}(0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3{t}^{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}2)⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{t},\,6t,\,0⟩ \\ {r}^{″}(0) & =⟨1,0,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the cross-product and its magnitude:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(0)\times {r}^{″}(0) & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}|i-|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}|j+|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}|k \\  & =2j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(0)\times {r}^{″}(0)‖ & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}}=2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the curvature at $t=0$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(0) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(0)\times {r}^{″}(0)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(0){‖}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{2}{(\sqrt{5})^{3}} \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{5}}{25}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=⟨{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,t⟩$ for $t\ge 0,$ use the cross product curvature formula to compute the curvature at the point $P(1,0,0).$
questions.worked_solution:
The curvature $κ(t)$ is given by

$$
κ(t)=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}.
$$

First, we find the value of $t$ that corresponds to the point $P(1,0,0)$ on the given curve. We know that

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨1,0,0⟩ \\ ⟨{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,t⟩ & =⟨1,0,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the respective components gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t=1 \\ {e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t=0 \\ t=0.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

From the third equality, $t=0.$ This value also satisfies the other two equations. Therefore, $P(1,0,0)$ is at the tip of $r(0).$ 

Now, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$, ${r}^{′}(0),$  and $‖{r}^{′}(0)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,{e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,1⟩ \\ {r}^{′}(0) & =⟨{e}^{0}\operatorname{cos}⁡0-{e}^{0}\operatorname{sin}⁡0,\,{e}^{-0}\operatorname{cos}⁡0-{e}^{-0}\operatorname{sin}⁡0,\,1⟩ \\  & =⟨1,1,1⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(0)‖ & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find ${r}^{″}(t)$ and ${r}^{″}(0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1)⟩ \\  & =⟨-2{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,-2{e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,0⟩ \\ {r}^{″}(0) & =⟨-2{e}^{0}\operatorname{sin}⁡0,\,-2{e}^{-0}\operatorname{cos}⁡0,\,0⟩⟩ \\  & =⟨0,-2,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the cross-product and its magnitude:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(0)\times {r}^{″}(0) & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & -2 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -2 & 0\end{aligned}|i-|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}|j+|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}|k \\  & =-2i-2k \\ ‖{r}^{′}(0)\times {r}^{″}(0)‖ & =\sqrt{(-2)^{2}+{0}^{2}+(-2)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4+0+4} \\  & =2\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the curvature at $t=0$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(0) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(0)\times {r}^{″}(0)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(0){‖}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{(\sqrt{3})^{3}} \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{3\sqrt{3}} \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{6}}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=⟨2t,\,{t}^{2},\,\operatorname{ln}⁡t⟩$ for $t>0$, use the cross product curvature formula to compute the curvature at the point $P(2,1,0).$
questions.worked_solution:
The curvature $κ(t)$ is given by

$$
κ(t)=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}.
$$

First, we find the value of $t$ that corresponds to the point $P(2,1,0)$ on the given curve. We know that

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨2,1,0⟩ \\ ⟨2t,\,{t}^{2},\,\operatorname{ln}⁡t⟩ & =⟨2,1,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the respective components gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}2t=2 \\ {t}^{2}=1 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡t=0.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equality, $t=1.$ This value also satisfies the other two equations. Therefore, $P(2,1,0)$ is at the tip of $r(1).$ 

Now, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$, ${r}^{′}(1),$  and $‖{r}^{′}(1)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨2,\,2t,\,\frac{1}{t}⟩ \\ {r}^{′}(1) & =⟨2,2,1⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(1)‖ & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}}=3\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find ${r}^{″}(t)$ and ${r}^{″}(1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{t})⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,2,\,-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}⟩ \\ {r}^{″}(1) & =⟨0,2,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the cross-product and its magnitude:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(1)\times {r}^{″}(1) & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 2 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}|i-|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}|j+|\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}|k \\  & =-4i+2j+4k \\ ‖{r}^{′}(1)\times {r}^{″}(1)‖ & =\sqrt{(-4)^{2}+{2}^{2}+{4}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{16+4+16} \\  & =6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the curvature at $t=1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(1) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(1)\times {r}^{″}(1)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(1){‖}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{6}{{3}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{2}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=⟨{e}^{t},\,{e}^{-t},\,2t⟩$ for $t\ge 0,$ use the cross product curvature formula to compute the curvature at the point $P(1,1,0).$
questions.worked_solution:
The curvature $κ(t)$ is given by

$$
κ(t)=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}.
$$

First, we find the value of $t$ that corresponds to the point $P(1,1,0)$ on the given curve. We know that

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨1,1,0⟩ \\ ⟨{e}^{t},\,{e}^{-t},\,2t⟩ & =⟨1,1,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the respective components gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}{e}^{t}=1 \\ {e}^{-t}=1 \\ 2t=0.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

From the third equality, $t=0.$ This value also satisfies the other two equations. Therefore, $P(1,1,0)$ is at the tip of $r(0).$ 

Now, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$, ${r}^{′}(0),$  and $‖{r}^{′}(0)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{-t}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t)⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{t},\,-{e}^{-t},\,2⟩ \\ {r}^{′}(0) & =⟨{e}^{0},-{e}^{-0},2⟩ \\  & =⟨1,-1,2⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(0)‖ & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+{2}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find ${r}^{″}(t)$ and ${r}^{″}(0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-{e}^{-t}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2)⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{t},\,{e}^{-t},\,0⟩ \\ {r}^{″}(0) & =⟨{e}^{0},{e}^{-0},0⟩ \\  & =⟨1,1,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the cross-product and its magnitude:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(0)\times {r}^{″}(0) & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & -1 & 2 \\ 1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}|i-|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}|j+|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}|k \\  & =-2i+2j+2k \\ ‖{r}^{′}(0)\times {r}^{″}(0)‖ & =\sqrt{(-2)^{2}+{2}^{2}+{2}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4+4+4} \\  & =2\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the curvature at $t=0$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(0) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(0)\times {r}^{″}(0)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(0){‖}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{(\sqrt{6})^{3}} \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{6\sqrt{6}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=⟨3\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,4t⟩$ for $0\le t<2\pi ,$ use the cross product curvature formula to compute the curvature at the point $P(0,-3,4\pi ).$
questions.worked_solution:
The curvature $κ(t)$ is given by

$$
κ(t)=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}.
$$

First, we find the value of $t$ that corresponds to the point $P(0,-3,4\pi )$ on the given curve. We know that

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨0,-3,4\pi ⟩ \\ ⟨3\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,4t⟩ & =⟨0,-3,4\pi ⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the respective components gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{sin}⁡t=0 \\ 3\operatorname{cos}⁡t=-3 \\ 4t=4\pi .\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

From the third equality, $t=\pi .$ This value also satisfies the other two equations. Therefore, $P(0,-3,4\pi )$ is at the tip of $r(\pi ).$ 

Now, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$, ${r}^{′}(\pi ),$  and $‖{r}^{′}(\pi )‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4t)⟩ \\  & =⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,4⟩ \\ {r}^{′}(\pi ) & =⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi ,-3\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi ,4⟩ \\  & =⟨-3,0,4⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(\pi )‖ & =\sqrt{(-3)^{2}+{0}^{2}+{4}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{25} \\  & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find ${r}^{″}(t)$ and ${r}^{″}(\pi ):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4)⟩ \\  & =⟨-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,-3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,0⟩ \\ {r}^{″}(\pi ) & =⟨-3\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi ,-3\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi ,0⟩ \\  & =⟨0,3,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the cross-product and its magnitude:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(\pi )\times {r}^{″}(\pi ) & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ -3 & 0 & 4 \\ 0 & 3 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}0 & 4 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}|i-|\begin{aligned}-3 & 4 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}|j+|\begin{aligned}-3 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}|k \\  & =-12i-9k \\  & =3(-4i-3k) \\ ‖{r}^{′}(\pi )\times {r}^{″}(\pi )‖ & =3\sqrt{(-4)^{2}+{0}^{2}+(-3)^{2}} \\  & =3\sqrt{16+9} \\  & =3(5) \\  & =15\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the curvature at $t=\pi $ is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(\pi ) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(\pi )\times {r}^{″}(\pi )‖}{‖{r}^{′}(\pi ){‖}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{15}{{5}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{3}{{5}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{3}{25}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,$ use the cross product curvature formula to find the curvature as a function of $t.$
questions.worked_solution:
The curvature $κ(t)$ is given by:

$$
κ(t)=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}\,\,
$$

First, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}+{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}+(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t+2{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the second derivative ${r}^{″}(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the cross-product and its magnitude:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t) & =⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\times ⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩ \\  & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡t & -\operatorname{sin}⁡t & \sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ -\operatorname{cos}⁡t & -\operatorname{cos}⁡t & -\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡t & \sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ -\operatorname{cos}⁡t & -\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}|i-|\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡t & \sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ -\operatorname{cos}⁡t & -\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}|j+|\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡t & -\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ -\operatorname{cos}⁡t & -\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}|k \\  & =\sqrt{2}i-\sqrt{2}j\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the magnitude of the above:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\sqrt{2})}^{2}+{(-\sqrt{2})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{2+2} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the curvature is:

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(t) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}=\frac{2}{(\sqrt{2})^{3}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=⟨-t,\,4,\,1+\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩$ for $0\le t\le \pi $, use the cross product curvature formula to find the curvature as a function of $t.$
questions.worked_solution:
The curvature $κ(t)$ is given by

$$
κ(t)=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}.
$$

First, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩=⟨-1,\,0,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+{0}^{2}+(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+{cos}^{2}⁡(t)}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the second derivative ${r}^{″}(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-1),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(0),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)⟩=⟨0,\,0,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the cross-product:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t) & =⟨-1,0,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\times ⟨0,0,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩ \\  & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ -1 & 0 & \operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ 0 & 0 & -\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}0 & \operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ 0 & -\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}|i-|\begin{aligned}-1 & \operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ 0 & -\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}|j+|\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}|k \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the magnitude of the above:

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖ & =|\operatorname{sin}⁡t|=\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $\operatorname{sin}⁡t\ge 0$ when $0\le t\le \pi .$

Therefore, the curvature is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(t) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{(1+{cos}^{2}⁡(t))^{3/2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(t) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}=\frac{18t}{{(3\sqrt{1+{t}^{4}})}^{3}}=\frac{2t}{3(1+{t}^{4})^{3/2}}.\end{aligned}

The curvature $κ(t)$ is given by

$$
κ(t)=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}.
$$

First, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$, ${r}^{′}(0),$ and $‖{r}^{′}(0)‖$:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{1-{t}^{2}}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{t}{\sqrt{1-{t}^{2}}},\,{e}^{t}⟩ \\ {r}^{′}(0) & =⟨-\frac{0}{\sqrt{1-{0}^{2}}},\,{e}^{0}⟩=⟨0,1⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(0)‖ & =\sqrt{{0}^{2}+{1}^{2}}=1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find ${r}^{″}(t)$ and ${r}^{″}(0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\frac{t}{\sqrt{1-{t}^{2}}}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{1}{{(1-{t}^{2})}^{3/2}},\,{e}^{t}⟩ \\ {r}^{″}(0) & =⟨-\frac{1}{(1-{0}^{2})^{3/2}},\,{e}^{0}⟩=⟨-1,\,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(0)\times {r}^{″}(0) & =⟨0,\,1,0⟩\times ⟨-1,\,1,\,0⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}\right|\,k \\  & =k \\ ‖{r}^{′}(0)\times {r}^{″}(0)‖ & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the curvature at $t=0$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(0) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(0)\times {r}^{″}(0)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(0){‖}^{3}}=\frac{1}{(1)^{3}}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

Notice that since $t>0$, we have $|t|=t.$

Now, we find the second derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3{t}^{2})⟩=⟨2,6t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the cross product by considering ${r}^{′}(t)$ and ${r}^{″}(t)$ as $3$-dimensional vectors with zero $z$-components:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t) & =⟨2t,\,3{t}^{2},\,0⟩\times ⟨2,\,6t,\,0⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 2t & 3{t}^{2} & 0 \\ 2 & 6t & 0\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}2t & 3{t}^{2} \\ 2 & 6t\end{aligned}\right|\,k \\  & =6{t}^{2}\,k\end{aligned}
$$

So, the magnitude of the cross product is

$$
‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖=6{t}^{2}.
$$

Therefore, the curvature is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(t) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{6{t}^{2}}{(t\sqrt{4+9{t}^{2}})^{3}} \\  & =\frac{6{t}^{2}}{{t}^{3}(4+9{t}^{2})^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{6}{t(4+9{t}^{2})^{3/2}}.\end{aligned}

questions.problem: Using the cross product curvature formula, find the curvature of $r(t)=⟨t\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,t\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩$ as a function of $t.$
questions.worked_solution:
The curvature $κ$ is given by

$$
κ(t)=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}.
$$

First, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖$:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t+t\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}+{(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{cos}^{2}⁡t-2t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+{t}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t+2t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+{t}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{{t}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t)+({cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =\sqrt{{t}^{2}+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find the second derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-t\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,2\operatorname{cos}⁡t-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the cross product by considering ${r}^{′}(t)$ and ${r}^{″}(t)$ as $3$-dimensional vectors with zero $z$-components:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t+t\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,0⟩\times ⟨-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-t\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,2\operatorname{cos}⁡t-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,0⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡t-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t & \operatorname{sin}⁡t+t\operatorname{cos}⁡t & 0 \\ -2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-t\operatorname{cos}⁡t & 2\operatorname{cos}⁡t-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t & 0\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡t-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t & \operatorname{sin}⁡t+t\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ -2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-t\operatorname{cos}⁡t & 2\operatorname{cos}⁡t-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{aligned}\right|\,k \\  & =[(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t)(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t+t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)]k \\  & =[2{cos}^{2}⁡t-3t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+{t}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡t+2{sin}^{2}⁡t+3t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t+{t}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡t]k \\  & =(2({cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t)+{t}^{2}({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t))k \\  & =({t}^{2}+2)k\end{aligned}
$$

So, the magnitude of the cross product is

$$
‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖={t}^{2}+2.
$$

Therefore, the curvature is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(t) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{{t}^{2}+2}{{(\sqrt{{t}^{2}+1})}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{{t}^{2}+2}{({t}^{2}+1)^{3/2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Using the cross product curvature formula, find the curvature of $r(t)=⟨t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩$ at the point where $t=\pi .$
questions.worked_solution:
The curvature $κ(t)$ is given by

$$
κ(t)=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}.
$$

First, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$, ${r}^{′}(\pi ),$ and $‖{r}^{′}(\pi )‖$:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩ \\ {r}^{′}(\pi ) & =⟨1-\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi ,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi ⟩=⟨2,0⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(\pi )‖ & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{0}^{2}}=2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find ${r}^{″}(t)$ and ${r}^{″}(\pi ):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩ \\ {r}^{″}(\pi ) & =⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi ,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi ⟩=⟨0,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the cross product by considering ${r}^{′}(\pi )$ and ${r}^{″}(\pi )$ as $3$-dimensional vectors with zero $z$-components:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(\pi )\times {r}^{″}(\pi ) & =⟨2,\,0,0⟩\times ⟨0,\,-1,\,0⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}\right|\,k \\  & =-2\,k \\ ‖{r}^{′}(\pi )\times {r}^{″}(\pi )‖ & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the curvature at $t=\pi $ is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(\pi ) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(\pi )\times {r}^{″}(\pi )‖}{‖{r}^{′}(\pi ){‖}^{3}}=\frac{2}{{2}^{3}}=\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}

canonical_examples.problem: Using the cross product curvature formula, find the curvature of $\mathbf r(t) = \langle t, -2t, t^2 \rangle$ at the point where $t = 1.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To compute the curvature $\kappa (t),$ we will use the following formula:

$$
\kappa(t) = \dfrac{\| \mathbf r'(t) \times \mathbf r''(t) \|}{\|\mathbf r'(t)\|^3}
$$

First, we calculate $\mathbf r'(t),$ $\mathbf r'(1),$ and $\|\mathbf r'(1)\|\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-2t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,-2,\,2t⟩ \\ {r}^{′}(1) & =⟨1,-2,2⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(1)‖ & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+(-2)^{2}+{2}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{9} \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find $\mathbf r''(t)$ and $\mathbf r''(1)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-2),2\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,0,2⟩ \\ {r}^{″}(1) & =⟨0,0,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the cross product and its magnitude:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(1)\times {r}^{″}(1) & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & -2 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}|i-|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}|j+|\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}|k \\  & =-4\,i-2\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(1)\times {r}^{″}(1)‖ & =\sqrt{(-4)^{2}+(-2)^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{20} \\  & =2\sqrt{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the curvature at $t=1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(1) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(1)\times {r}^{″}(1)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(1){‖}^{3}}=\frac{2\sqrt{5}}{{3}^{3}}=\frac{2\sqrt{5}}{27}.\end{aligned}
$$

The curvature $\kappa (t)$ is given by

$$
\kappa(t) = \dfrac{\| \mathbf r'(t) \times \mathbf r''(t) \|}{\|\mathbf r'(t)\|^3} .

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1)⟩ \\  & =⟨2t,\,2,\,0⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{(2t)^{2}+(2)^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+4} \\  & =\sqrt{4({t}^{2}+1)} \\  & =2\sqrt{{t}^{2}+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the second derivative $\mathbf{r}''(t)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(0)⟩=⟨2,\,0,\,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the cross-product:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t) & =⟨2t,2,0⟩\times ⟨2,0,0⟩ \\  & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 2t & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}|i-|\begin{aligned}2t & 0 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}|j+|\begin{aligned}2t & 2 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}|k \\  & =-4\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the magnitude of the above:

$$

$$

$$
